svg.title: Speed at a glance – where the databases really differ
svg.desc: Users would notice a difference in 12 of these 29 tests (8 of them in Platform basics: bulk record work). Noticeably slower: MySQL in 11 of them, PostgreSQL in 7, SQL Server in 1. Everything else is a tie. Noticeable differences: Deep paging and counting in a 300,000-line journal: MySQL 70% slower (+19.9 s vs SQL Server); Enter sales orders – 1 clerk: MySQL 20% slower (+145 ms vs SQL Server), PostgreSQL 15% slower (+108 ms vs SQL Server); Enter sales orders – 8 clerks working non-stop: MySQL 10% slower (vs PostgreSQL only); Create and release invoices to the GL – 1 person: MySQL 43% slower (+391 ms vs SQL Server), PostgreSQL 30% slower (+270 ms vs SQL Server); Load 10,000 records – 1 worker: SQL Server 1.98× slower (+0.108 s vs PostgreSQL), MySQL 2.33× slower (+0.148 s vs PostgreSQL); Save 10,000 new records – 1 worker: MySQL 23% slower (+1.77 s vs SQL Server), PostgreSQL 56% slower (+4.25 s vs SQL Server); Save 10,000 new records – one job shared by 8 parallel workers: PostgreSQL 23% slower (vs MySQL only); Change 10,000 records – 1 worker: MySQL 23% slower (+1.3 s vs SQL Server), PostgreSQL 44% slower (+2.5 s vs SQL Server); Delete 10,000 records – 1 worker: MySQL 54% slower (+12.9 s vs SQL Server), PostgreSQL 55% slower (+13.3 s vs SQL Server); Delete 10,000 records – one job shared by 8 parallel workers: MySQL 22% slower (vs SQL Server only); Stock availability list, only the needed columns – 1 worker: MySQL 37% slower (+8.89 ms vs SQL Server), PostgreSQL 43% slower (+10.2 ms vs SQL Server); Stock availability list, only the needed columns – one job shared by 8 parallel workers: MySQL 48% slower (+5.87 ms vs PostgreSQL). Each cell shows the median for one database and a verdict chip: fastest, a percentage slower, or tie.

g.font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', 'Helvetica Neue', Helvetica, Arial, 'Liberation Sans', sans-serif
g.text: Speed at a glance – where the databases really differ
Users would notice a difference in 12 of these 29 tests (8 of them in Platform basics: bulk record work).
Noticeably slower: MySQL in 11 of them, PostgreSQL in 7, SQL Server in 1.
A chip is coloured only where a difference is both real (consistent across the 6 runs) and big enough for users to notice. It then
takes the colour of the database in that column.
in the fastest group, but ties with every other database
failed saves or a different answer
Grey notes explain ties that look like gaps: the extra time is too small to feel, the gap is within the normal run-to-run swings, or that database’s own runs

text.tspan: No noticeable difference in any of the 4 tests
